1. *"the course—East-south-east— which he was to steer, if practicable, was once more given to the helmsman; for during the violence of the gale, he had only steered according to its vicissitudes."* — The "for" clause is preserved from source. Fine.

2. The draft cuts Starbuck's monologue line: *"But if I wake thee not to death, old man, who can tell to what unsounded deeps Starbuck's body this day week may sink, with all the crew!"* — This appears between "boy! boy! boy!—" and "Great God, where art Thou?" in the source. The draft goes directly from "boy! boy! boy!—" to "Great God, where art Thou?" The connective logic still parses; it's a cut interior reflection. The remaining sentences still stand. Not a structural damage.

3. *"Such were the sounds from the old man's tormented sleep."* — Source: *"Such were the sounds that now came hurtling from out the old man's tormented sleep, as if Starbuck's voice had caused the long dumb dream to speak."* The draft drops the gloss "as if Starbuck's voice had caused the long dumb dream to speak." This gloss explains *why* Ahab suddenly cries out — it's the causal mechanism explaining how Ahab's dream-speech is triggered by Starbuck's report. Without it, Ahab's outburst ("Stern all! Oh Moby Dick…") appears as a non-sequitur response to Starbuck rather than an eruption from sleep. A reader might genuinely be confused about whether Ahab has woken up and is speaking consciously. But the draft does say "tormented sleep," so the reader knows Ahab is asleep. This is ornamentation cut, not structural damage. The reader understands it's sleep-speech.

4. *"He's too sound asleep, Mr. Stubb; go thou down, and wake him…"* — In the source, this is Starbuck addressing Stubb after leaving the cabin. In the draft, the preceding text has Starbuck leaving the cabin ("left the place") and then this dialogue appears. Stubb has not been introduced or established as present in the draft of Ch 126. However, Stubb was named earlier in Ch 126 draft ("Starbuck and Stubb—one forward, the other aft") so he is a known character in the draft. The dialogue is Starbuck addressing Stubb, but Stubb's presence at this moment (outside the cabin) is not established in the draft — yet this is also true in the source; the source doesn't establish Stubb as physically present at the cabin either. It's simply Starbuck finding someone to send. A competent reader would understand Starbuck is delegating to Stubb. Not a structural damage.
